problem:
Express $z=\sqrt{3}-\text{i}$ in the form $r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ).$ Give the **exact** values of $r$ and $\theta ,$ in **radians** from $[0,2\pi ).$

$z=$
{{field-1}}$\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(${{field-2}}$)+\,i\operatorname{sin}⁡(${{field-3}}$))$

feedback.worked_solution:
First, we express the given complex number in the form $z=x+y\text{i}.$ We get

$$
z=0+(-2)\text{i}.
$$

In polar form, $r$ represents the magnitude $|z|.$ For a complex number $z=x+y\text{i},$ the magnitude of $z$ is given by

$$
|z|=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.
$$

So, for $z=0+(-2)\text{i},$ the magnitude is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=|z| & =\sqrt{{(0)}^{2}+{(-2)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

      

In polar form, $\theta $  represents the argument $\operatorname{arg}⁡(z).$ Since $x=0$  and $y=-2$ is negative, $z$ lies on the negative $y$-axis. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta =\operatorname{arg}⁡(z) & =\frac{3\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the complex number $z=-2\text{i}$ in polar form:

$$
z=2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}))
$$
